sources.title: Dagbovie: Woodson’s historical programme and critical reception (2012)
sources.citation: Pero Gaglo Dagbovie, “Willing to Sacrifice”: Carter G. Woodson, the Father of Black History, and the Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site, Historic Resource Study (National Park Service, April2012), selected printed17–21,29,33,96–97,99–110,175–177.

verification.note: Fresh selected named scholarly analysis, not a new reading of the original documents reproduced or cited. Printed17–18 and n29 substantively reconstruct Du Bois’s1922 church-history criticism and preserve praise. Pages21/n48 identify Woodson’s1919 Phillips review;29/33 and175–177 support held funding, mentoring and reception leads. Most study pages and cited originals unread. PDF title page dates April2012; current web-upload/search dates are not publication dates.

sources.title: Du Bois: Woodson’s textbook as a teaching resource (1935)
sources.citation: W. E. Burghardt Du Bois, “Does the Negro Need Separate Schools?,” The Journal of Negro Education4,no.3(July1935),328–335; National Humanities Center-hosted scan, especially333 and335.

verification.note: Fresh selected primary page333 and conclusion335 read. Du Bois names the first edition of Woodson’s textbook alongside other authors and Negro History Week. The first edition and other named books remain unread. Own authorial argument distinguished from the later Wesley/Perry introduction that had supplied a discovery lead.

sources.title: Higginbotham: oral-history account of Woodson’s mediated influence (2011/2012)
sources.citation: Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham, interview by Enimini Ekong,16June2011, transcribed by Ashley Robertson, in Pero Gaglo Dagbovie, “Willing to Sacrifice” (NPS,April2012), appendixA,185–188.

verification.note: Fresh selected respondent’s own transcript read: heading185 identifies date/interviewer/transcriber;185 directly identifies her father’s devotion to Woodson as leading her into history;188 distinguishes inherited knowledge, later reading and the missing women’s perspective. Interview recording not heard; other speakers in appendix not assigned to Higginbotham. Father Albert N. D. Brooks retains intermediary credit.
